cards.title: Prioritize core lifecycle flows over advanced segmentation
cards.summary: Build the seven basic email flows — welcome, site abandon, browse abandon, cart abandon, checkout abandon, post-purchase and win-back — before advanced segmentations.
cards.use_when: Planning your store's email lifecycle roadmap or deciding where to invest automation effort first.
steps: Adopt the seven core flows as your baseline stack: welcome (8 emails), site abandon (1 email), browse abandon (5 emails), cart abandon (6-8 emails), checkout abandon (6-8 emails), post-purchase (3+ emails) and win-back (3 emails).
Resist the urge to build complex hypersegmentation first — per the source, advanced segmentation 'takes a lot of effort for not as many results' as nailing the basics.
Treat the email counts and delays below as starting templates, not proven optima; the source explicitly says every brand must test.
Set each flow to fire on its own distinct trigger and use exit filters so a customer moves through the funnel rather than receiving overlapping flows.
After launch, move improvement effort into campaign testing (see the campaign-as-testing-ground card) rather than endless flow surgery.
caveats: The flow counts and delays are the presenter's base outlines for 7-8 figure brands, not universal benchmarks — you must test per account.

cards.title: Welcome flow: 8-email structure with exit filter
cards.summary: A 4-10 email welcome series delivering your acquisition discount, brand story, hero products and social proof, with a purchase filter removing buyers mid-flow.
cards.use_when: Setting up the new-subscriber welcome automation after your popup/form captures an email.
steps: Trigger on someone joining your email list; add a filter that exits anyone who makes a purchase (0 purchases since starting the flow) so buyers don't keep receiving discount prompts and instead enter the post-purchase flow.
Email 1: strong introduction — deliver the welcome discount at the top of the email (not buried), plus USPs, light social proof and best sellers; keep it condensed.
Email 2: brand background — founding story, face to the name, team photo, and sprinkle social proof into the story.
Email 3: highlight best sellers and why they're good, reminding of the discount.
Email 4: urgency — discount is expiring soon, add risk reversals (guarantees, shipping promise) and testimonials.
Email 5: us-versus-them — clearly list why you differ from competitors the subscriber is likely also evaluating.
Email 6: heavy social proof — brand testimonials and any media features.
Email 7: last chance, kept super simple and aggressive.
Email 8: note from the founder — check in, offer support via reply, and offer an extended discount (source says this email usually does well).
Use 1-2 day delays between emails (source sometimes uses 2-3 days); remind recipients of the discount in every email.
caveats: Source acknowledges discomfort with discounting first purchase but argues list value repays it; that is an opinion, not measured proof.
Offer the founder a real reply channel only if you can handle responses.

cards.title: Welcome flow's two acceptable outcomes
cards.summary: Design the welcome flow to either convert the curious subscriber or prime a future buyer whose objections are already answered.
cards.use_when: Setting success metrics and email content priorities for the welcome automation.
steps: Outcome A: convert subscribers who would otherwise have left, using a strong popup form plus a welcome flow that addresses objections as they arrive.
Outcome B: if they don't buy, treat the flow as objection-priming — deliver the information needed so that when the need arises, campaigns convert without fresh objection handling.
Keep every email discount-visible so both outcomes retain the incentive thread.
After the flow completes, move non-buyers into the regular campaign list rather than leaving them in the automation.
caveats: Outcome B is hard to measure directly; treat it as a content-hygiene principle rather than an attribution claim.

cards.title: Site abandon flow: one-email nudge to keep browsing
cards.summary: A single email sent 2-4 hours after a site visit with no product view, aimed at re-engaging or routing visitors down the funnel.
cards.use_when: Adding a recovery flow for visitors who hit your homepage or category pages and leave without viewing a product.
steps: Trigger on 'active on site' (the source uses Klaviyo/Shopify); exit anyone who views a product, adds to cart, reaches checkout, or purchases, so they enter the deeper flows instead.
Add a suppression so a visitor can't receive this flow more than once in 30 days.
Wait 2-4 hours before sending; the source found this window best but says to test it.
Send one email: 'Do you need some help?' — remind them to keep shopping and surface best sellers, a few categories, and light social proof.
Keep the email deliberately simple — don't overload it; the goal is to push them deeper into the funnel, not to sell a specific item.
caveats: Site-visit frequency is low per visitor, so send consistency matters more than frequency here.
An exit-filter misconfiguration can cause visitors to receive this alongside deeper abandon flows.

cards.title: Browse abandon flow: 5-email recap that escalates slowly
cards.summary: A 5-email sequence for product viewers who didn't add to cart or buy, starting with a fast reminder and saving discounts for later.
cards.use_when: Building the browse-abandonment automation for shoppers who viewed a PDP but didn't add to cart.
steps: Trigger on viewed product; exit anyone who adds to cart, starts checkout, or purchases; suppress repeat entrants for 30 days.
Wait 45 minutes before the first email (source says test the interval). Email 1 shows the exact product they viewed via dynamic content (e.g., Klaviyo's dynamic block) with a simple reminder.
Email 2 (1-2 days later): brand info and risk reversals, plus other products they can shop — the objection is buy-in on the brand.
Email 3: testimonials and social proof on the viewed item, with dynamic content showing what they abandoned.
Email 4: introduce a discount only after the free options — the source deliberately delays discounting to protect margins — framed as a 48-hour flash.
Email 5: short closer, 'expires in 24 hours', discount reminder.
Keep emails very simple and use dynamic blocks in each email so the visitor sees their actual product.
caveats: Do not wait a week — source says this is too long while attention is fresh.
Discount timing is a margin trade-off, not a proven revenue lift for your account; test.

cards.title: Cart abandon and checkout abandon are two separate flows
cards.summary: Add-to-cart and checkout-start abandonment need distinct triggers and exit filters, even if they reuse the same email content.
cards.use_when: Auditing or building cart and checkout recovery automations.
steps: Recognize the difference: adding to cart is a different event from entering the payment/shipping checkout page, so each needs its own flow.
Cart abandon trigger: added to cart; exit filters should include 'placed order 0 times' and 'checkout started' so anyone further down the funnel enters checkout abandon instead.
Checkout abandon triggers on checkout start with its own exit filter on purchase.
Reuse the same email content across both flows — the source uses identical content with different triggers.

Source claims roughly 90% of brands audited lack a proper cart-abandon flow; verify your platform actually fires an abandoned-cart trigger (the source says Klaviyo added it via Shopify integration around September 2024) or build a custom trigger.
Run 6-8 emails; first email ~30 minutes after the trigger (source's recommendation, test it), then 1-2 day gaps.
caveats: Platform trigger availability changes — verify the current interface and event names in your platform before assuming it exists.

cards.title: Cart/checkout abandon content sequence
cards.summary: Email-by-email content plan for cart and checkout abandonment that ends with tiered offers for first-time versus returning buyers.
cards.use_when: Writing the emails inside cart-abandon and checkout-abandon flows.
steps: Email 1: simple reminder of the abandoned product with a shop-now CTA and dynamic block showing the item.
Email 2: text-based nudge from the founder — informal, personal, 'you left something behind'.
Email 3: brand USPs and why to choose you over other stores the shopper is likely comparing.
Email 4: customer testimonials plus dynamic abandoned content.
Email 5: last-chance urgency — 'your order is expiring, we can't hold it much longer'.

Branch the final email: returning buyers get a founder check-in with support offer, no discount; first-time buyers get a discount opener (e.g., '15% off if you buy within 48 hours') followed by a founder 'everything okay?' discount closer.
Place the dynamic abandoned-product block at the top of every email and add cross-sell recommendations at the bottom.
caveats: The 15% / 48-hour figures are examples from the source, not calibrated thresholds for your store.
Discounting checkout abandoners can train customers to abandon deliberately — consider testing versus a no-discount branch.

cards.title: Post-purchase flow: 3 emails that thank, bond, and enable
cards.summary: A short post-purchase sequence: immediate founder thank-you with add-on offer, social follow, then product-usage tips that drive repeat purchase.
cards.use_when: Building the automation that fires immediately after an order is placed.
steps: Trigger on order placed with no exit filter — everyone should receive it.

Email 1, sent immediately: text-based thank-you from the founder using the customer's first name, tying the order to your mission, offering support by reply, and including a PS add-to-order offer within 24 hours — the source calls this an immediate big purchase window.
Email 2, ~2 days later: invite them to your main social channel or community group to grow your owned audience.

Email 3, ~3 days later: 'how to get the most from your product' — usage tips, routines, pairing suggestions that naturally set up the upsell, plus a recommended-products block based on customer activity.
Keep it to about three emails; the source says four-plus is optional and three is fine.
caveats: The add-to-order offer window depends on your fulfillment speed; if orders ship same-day, combine the add-on offer into the order confirmation instead.

cards.title: Win-back flow: fire at double the average repurchase interval
cards.summary: A simple 3-email re-engagement sequence timed at roughly twice the customer's average time between purchases.
cards.use_when: Setting up reactivation automation for customers who bought months ago.
steps: Set the trigger based on elapsed time since last order — if average time between purchases is ~45 days, fire at ~90 days (source's rule of thumb: double the interval), or use 60/90/120 days.
Exit anyone who makes a purchase after entering the flow.
Email 1: 'it's been a while' brand reminder with a comeback nudge and a dynamic recommendation based on the customer's last purchase.
Email 2 (about a week later): a unique, dynamically generated discount code per customer — the source says personalized codes convert better.
Email 3: text-based last-chance from the founder, warm and understanding, restating the expiring discount.
Keep the flow simple; the source argues most repeat purchases come from regular campaigns (3-4 sends per week), not the win-back flow, so treat it partly as customer experience.
caveats: The double-the-interval rule is a heuristic, not a measured formula, and only works if you have a reliable average repurchase interval.
Source's claim that ~99% of retention/repeat revenue comes from campaigns is the presenter's assertion, not a verified benchmark for your list.

cards.title: Use campaigns as the testing ground for flow content
cards.summary: Rather than running many A/B tests inside flows, test angles in frequent campaigns and port winning emails into flows.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to optimize lifecycle emails when flow testing is slow and hard to track.
steps: Send 3-4 email campaigns per week (minimum 2) so you get fast, 24-hour data on angles and subject lines.

Track campaign performance; when an email wins, add its angle to the relevant flow: educational product-creation emails to the welcome flow (with discount added), usage-tip emails to the post-purchase flow, return-policy emails to the cart-abandon flow for risk reversal.
Avoid maintaining dozens of simultaneous active tests across triggers — the source says flows are hard to monitor at scale and need spreadsheets to track.
Only accept flow-specific test results when the sample is meaningful; wait for customer entry volume before judging a flow variant.
Document what went into which flow so you don't re-test identical angles repeatedly.
caveats: Campaign and flow audiences behave differently, so a campaign winner is a strong hypothesis, not a guaranteed flow winner.

cards.title: Test flow time delays before content
cards.summary: Time delay from customer action to first email is described as the biggest, fastest lever in flow testing.
cards.use_when: Choosing and tuning send delays for site, browse, cart and checkout abandon flows.
steps: Pick one abandonment flow and test two delays for the first email — e.g., the source compared 30 minutes versus 4 hours for a website-abandon flow.

Evaluate on placed-order rate, not just opens: in the source's example, the 30-minute delay got better open and click rates, but the 4-hour delay produced a much higher placed-order rate on a large sample.
Do not assume faster is always better — the source explicitly says the placed-order result favored waiting longer in that case.
Apply findings per flow, since attention windows differ (browse: 45 minutes recommended; cart: ~30 minutes; site: 2-4 hours; win-back: weeks).
Re-test delays as your list and traffic composition change.
caveats: The 30-minute versus 4-hour comparison is one case study; the source calls it a large sample but it does not establish a universal best delay.

cards.title: Long-form versus short-form flow emails
cards.summary: Test whether abandonment emails should walk through objections or just remind — short reminders often win on impulse purchases.
cards.use_when: Deciding email length and content depth in abandonment flows and campaigns.
steps: Test a long email that explicitly works through objections against a short one that just says 'you left this behind, shop now'.

In the source's comparison on ~2,000 recipients, the short email achieved a 0.2% placed-order rate and 2.4% click rate versus better performance for the quick reminder — use this as a hypothesis, not a rule.
Reason about intent: some abandoners need their objections talked through, while others have no objections and only need a reminder — segment or sequence accordingly.
Combine both in sequence where possible: short reminder first, longer objection-handling email later in the flow.
Judge by placed-order rate, not click rate alone, since long educational emails can earn clicks without purchases.
caveats: Single A/B example, not a universal result; the source stresses it must be tested per account.

cards.title: Subject line and preview text tests to run
cards.summary: Specific subject-line variables worth A/B testing: discounts mentioned, emojis, ellipses, caps, and length.
cards.use_when: Running subject line experiments for campaigns or flow emails.
steps: Test including versus excluding discount mentions (e.g., 'sale').
Test including versus excluding emojis in subject lines and preview text.
Test ellipses ('...') versus plain endings.
Test ALL CAPS versus sentence case.
Test different urgency timeframes stated in the subject line.

Remember the source's caveat: subject-line test learnings are hard to transfer to future emails because so much varies — use them for immediate improvement rather than building a permanent subject-line rulebook.
caveats: High variability makes subject-line learnings less durable; expect to keep re-testing.

cards.title: Graphic-heavy versus text-based email design
cards.summary: Text-based founder-style emails often outperform graphic-heavy ones, but the source says to balance and test.
cards.use_when: Choosing email format for flow emails such as founder nudges, thank-yous and last-chance messages.
steps: Build a plain-text-style email (little or no imagery) that reads as a personal message, e.g., a founder note sign-off.
Compare it against your standard template with heavy graphics on open rate, click rate and revenue.
In the source's example, the text-based founder email beat the graphic email on opens, clicks and revenue — treat this as a directional hypothesis for your list.
Use text-based design preferentially for personal messages — founder notes, thank-yous, cart nudges, win-back last chances — and keep graphic design for product showcases and social proof blocks.
Re-test when you see sales drops or list composition changes.
caveats: Performance varies by account; the source explicitly says to test rather than assume text always wins.

cards.title: Promoting categories versus individual products in email
cards.summary: Test category-level promotion against specific-product promotion — higher-ticket stores in the source leaned toward categories.
cards.use_when: Deciding what to feature in campaign and flow email blocks, especially for higher-ticket catalogs.
steps: Create one variant featuring specific products ('shop this jacket') and one featuring categories ('shop jackets, shop pants').
Measure clicks and revenue, not just clicks.
In the source's higher-ticket store example, categories produced higher clicks and higher revenue, so they biased future emails toward category promotion.
Default to individual products when the flow is abandonment-driven and you can show the exact abandoned item dynamically.
Revisit the bias as catalog breadth and price points change.
caveats: Single-store example; the source presents it as a tested bias, not a universal rule.

cards.title: Seed welcome-flow social proof with early testimonials
cards.summary: Use whatever review volume and testimonials you have, and place them where the sequence's doubts peak.
cards.use_when: Writing welcome-flow emails when you have a new or small brand with little social proof.
steps: Place light social proof in email 1, woven into the founder story rather than isolated.
Save the heavy-proof email (brand testimonials, media features) for email 6, after brand education and before the aggressive last-chance email.
Use existing proof even if modest — the source suggests sprinkling review counts or media mentions into the story rather than waiting for large numbers.
Add testimonials to the urgency email (email 4) for recipients still on the fence, and repeat proof inside browse/cart recovery emails for the exact item abandoned.
Do not fabricate proof; if the brand is new, use founder credibility and risk reversal instead of numerical claims.
caveats: The source does not prescribe a minimum review count — do not invent one.

cards.title: Founder-message emails and when they convert
cards.summary: Persona-driven 'note from the founder' emails work across welcome, abandonment and win-back flows when kept simple and human.
cards.use_when: Writing personal-voice emails for welcome close, cart abandon, post-purchase thanks or win-back final send.
steps: Use the founder (or a named person) as sender with the customer's first name in the body.
Keep it short and text-based; the source says these perform well because recipients feel personally reached.
Offer a real support channel: invite recipients to reply to the email with questions.
In abandonment flows, use it as the second email or the last-chance email, offering support and occasionally extending the discount by a day.
In post-purchase, use it immediately after order placed to convey mission and offer add-ons within 24 hours.
Expect and prepare for support replies — the source notes these emails generate customer questions.
caveats: Requires a real inbox and response process; unmonitored replies can hurt trust.
Founder credibility must be genuine — do not invent a persona.

cards.title: Customize flows with dynamic product blocks
cards.summary: Use platform dynamic content so recovery and recommendation emails show the exact product or a personalized suggestion per recipient.
cards.use_when: Building browse-abandon, cart-abandon, post-purchase and win-back emails in Klaviyo or a comparable platform.
steps: Add a dynamic block showing the abandoned product (image, name, price, link) at the top of browse and cart/checkout abandonment emails.
Use the platform's product-recommendation blocks based on the customer's activity in post-purchase and win-back emails.
Generate per-customer dynamic discount codes in win-back flows so each recipient feels their offer is unique — the source says these convert better.
In welcome-flow examples, keep discount code visible throughout; a generic graphic won't reproduce that per-recipient effect.
Verify the current name and setup of dynamic blocks in your platform, as interfaces change.
caveats: Dynamic blocks depend on your catalog and event data being clean; missing product data produces blank or wrong recommendations.

cards.title: Run 3-4 email campaigns per week to carry retention
cards.summary: Regular campaigns, not just flows, drive most repeat purchases; keep send frequency at least two per week.
cards.use_when: Planning weekly retention calendar and deciding how much to rely on automation versus broadcasts.
steps: Send 3-4 campaigns per week (the source treats two as the floor).
Use these campaigns as your testing ground for angles that later get ported into flows.
Keep the win-back flow simple because recipients are still receiving your regular campaigns.
Expect most repeat purchases to come from campaigns — the source asserts around 99% of retention and repeat purchases, but treat this as the presenter's claim, not a measured figure for your list.
Watch engagement and unsubscribes when scaling frequency; adjust if list health degrades.
caveats: The 99% claim is an unverified assertion in the source; do not plan forecasts around it.

cards.title: Risk reversal and urgency placement in sequence
cards.summary: Place urgency and risk reversals at the sequence point where they resolve the remaining objection, not in the first email.
cards.use_when: Ordering content in welcome, browse, cart and checkout abandonment sequences.
steps: In the welcome flow, deliver the incentive first, then USPs/product education, then social proof, then urgency ('discount expiring soon') with risk reversal (30-day guarantee, shipping promise), then heavy proof, then last chance.
In browse abandon, keep email 1 as a pure reminder, put risk reversal in email 2, and put the discount in email 4 with a 48-hour framing.
In cart/checkout abandon, keep the last chance email separate from the discount branch, giving returning buyers a no-discount founder note instead.
In win-back, reserve the unique discount for email 2 and the last-chance founder note for email 3.
Use short, specific urgency ('expires in 24 hours') rather than vague pressure.
caveats: Aggressive urgency in the last email may cost list goodwill; the source recommends testing timing and tone.
